clinical_category: Pursed-lip breathing in COPD - dyspnea relief and prolonged expiration
blueprint_topic: Nonpharmacologic breathing technique for comfort and symptom control in obstructive lung disease
stem: A nurse teaches a client with COPD to use pursed-lip breathing during episodes of breathlessness. Which explanation of the technique is accurate?

options.A: Slow exhalation through pursed lips prolongs expiration and creates slight expiratory backpressure that can reduce air trapping and the sensation of dyspnea
options.B: The technique works mainly by causing rapid shallow breathing and shortening the expiratory phase
options.C: Pursed-lip breathing replaces prescribed bronchodilator therapy when COPD symptoms increase
options.D: The technique intentionally promotes small-airway collapse during exhalation so trapped air remains in the lungs

rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI/StatPearls guidance describes pursed-lip breathing as a slow, controlled exhalation through pursed lips that prolongs the expiratory phase and generates a small amount of positive expiratory pressure. This backpressure helps resist airway collapse, supports more complete exhalation, reduces air trapping, decreases work of breathing, and can relieve dyspnea. B and D describe the opposite of the intended expiratory mechanics. C is incorrect because pursed-lip breathing is a supportive nonpharmacologic technique and does not replace prescribed COPD medications. The final item does not claim a universal improvement in exercise tolerance because response to the technique can vary by population and clinical context.
educational_objective: Teach pursed-lip breathing as a supportive COPD breathing technique that prolongs controlled exhalation, creates slight expiratory backpressure, reduces air trapping and work of breathing, and can lessen dyspnea without replacing prescribed therapy.
source_version_date: StatPearls; last update 2025-01-25; current 2026 NCBI Bookshelf edition accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf 'Pursed-lip Breathing' → Definition/Introduction: deliberate nasal inhalation followed by slow controlled exhalation through pursed lips prolongs expiration and generates a small amount of positive end-expiratory pressure; the backpressure helps prevent airway collapse and reduces air trapping. Clinical Significance: pursed-lip breathing can reduce work of breathing and alleviate dyspnea; effectiveness varies across patient populations, supporting individualized use rather than a universal functional-outcome claim.
source_claim_supported: Current NCBI/StatPearls content directly supports prolonged controlled exhalation, slight expiratory backpressure, reduced airway collapse/air trapping, reduced work of breathing, and dyspnea relief as the pursed-lip-breathing construct tested by the item.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort client-needs subcategory (6–12% of items), within Physiological Integrity; this item tests a nonpharmacologic comfort and breathing-support intervention used to reduce respiratory distress.
correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. The source item used a secondary association resource and combined dyspnea relief with a broad exercise-tolerance claim. The final item uses current NCBI/StatPearls guidance and limits the answer to directly supported expiratory mechanics, reduced air trapping/work of breathing, and dyspnea relief, while explicitly avoiding a universal exercise-capacity claim.
audit_findings: The source item used a secondary patient-education source despite an adequate current NCBI/StatPearls mechanism source.
Current StatPearls directly supports prolonged expiration, slight positive expiratory pressure, resistance to airway collapse, reduced air trapping, reduced work of breathing, and dyspnea relief.
The original exercise-tolerance claim was removed because the evidence summarized in the current source varies by patient population and does not justify a universal outcome statement.
Distractors test shortened expiration, medication replacement, and promoted airway collapse; all directly conflict with the verified mechanism or appropriate role.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no second defensible option, no unsupported exercise-performance claim, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
